correctness.rationale: The rational Zak numerator is P(x)+Q(x)e^{2πiω}, with Q/P strictly increasing from zero to infinity, so its only zero is at ω=1/2 and P=Q. At this zero the two unnormalized derivative columns are −(a+b)A and −2πiβA; the normalization multiplies the real determinant by 2ab/(a+b). Thus J=4πabβA², and local change of variables plus the positive modulus away from the zero gives π/J as the sharp area coefficient. The coefficient of δ² in the fixed-sum logarithm is 1/(4q²)−tanh(q)/(2q)+sech²(q)/2; the equivalent threshold function is strictly increasing by sinh(q)cosh(q)>q. Boundary divergence gives attained minima and excludes balance above the threshold. For the large-rate limit, sC is bounded below by e^{a/2}/(4a) on a≤s/2 and admits a bounded fixed-a comparison, giving compactness of all smaller minimizing rates. On such compact sets A→1/(1+e^a), β→1/(1+e^{−a}) uniformly, giving F(a); its derivative equation has exactly one root, which implies the limit for every selection of minimizers. An independent replay reproduced the three numerical constants and checked Zak sums and determinants; it is corroboration, not the limiting proof.
residual_risks: Fixed positive rates are used in the small-area limit. No strict extremum at the threshold, global balance below it, or exhaustive finite-s classification is asserted.

value.rationale: The sharp area coefficient measures how much of a normalized Zak cell has small transform magnitude, beyond simply detecting the zero. The fixed-budget local switch and the global all-minimizer limit explain when and how unequal rates improve this statistic; the surviving smaller decay tends to a specific finite value rather than tracking the growing total rate.
residual_risks: This area law is not itself an exact oversampled frame bound; no such downstream significance is needed.
